title: Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism

questions.title: Price-Taking Behavior in a Small Open Economy
questions.prompt_template: In the canonical single-market model of international trade, what does the 'small open economy' assumption mean for the world price (P_w)?

hints.text: Think about whether a single small country's purchases or sales are large enough to move global market-clearing prices.
Compare this assumption to a perfectly competitive firm facing a horizontal market price line.

options_template.text: The country's domestic equilibrium price always equals the world price even before opening to trade.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Autarky-Trade Conflation): Before opening to trade, the autarky price P_A generally differs from P_w; that price gap is what drives trade.

options_template.text: The country is a price-taker in the world market and can buy or sell any quantity at P_w without altering the global price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A small open economy represents a negligible share of global demand or supply, so foreign supply or demand at P_w is effectively perfectly elastic.

options_template.text: The country has no domestic producers and must import 100% of its consumption at P_w.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Domestic Supply Assumption): A small open economy still has an upward-sloping domestic supply curve; domestic firms simply produce less when P_w < P_A.

options_template.text: The country's government fixes the world price by setting domestic price ceilings and floors.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Global Price Control Error): A small country cannot dictate global prices; domestic policies only change its internal price relative to P_w.

questions.title: Determining Whether a Country Imports or Exports
questions.prompt_template: How does comparing a small open economy's autarky equilibrium price (P_A) with the world price (P_w) reveal comparative advantage and trade direction?

hints.text: Remember that a lower autarky price reflects a lower domestic opportunity cost of producing the good.
Check which side of the market has an incentive to buy abroad versus sell abroad when borders open.

options_template.text: If P_w < P_A, foreign producers have a comparative advantage and the country imports the good; if P_w > P_A, domestic producers have a comparative advantage and the country exports it.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A lower price reflects lower opportunity cost, so P_w < P_A signals foreign comparative advantage (importing) and P_w > P_A signals domestic comparative advantage (exporting).

options_template.text: If P_w < P_A, domestic producers have a comparative advantage and export the good; if P_w > P_A, the country imports it.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade Direction Reversal): When the world price is below the domestic autarky price, foreign producers are cheaper, so domestic buyers import rather than export.

options_template.text: The country exports whenever its domestic autarky quantity Q_A exceeds zero, regardless of P_w.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Volume-Only Criterion): Trade direction depends on relative opportunity costs (P_A vs. P_w), not on whether domestic production exists under autarky.

options_template.text: The country imports only when P_w = P_A, because equality guarantees balanced trade.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Trade Equilibrium Confusion): When P_w = P_A, domestic quantity demanded equals domestic quantity supplied, so zero trade occurs.

questions.title: Why Importing Increases Total Social Surplus
questions.prompt_template: A common objection to free trade is that imports harm national welfare because they reduce domestic producer surplus. Why does welfare economics conclude that importing at P_w < P_A raises Total Social Surplus?

hints.text: Compare the magnitude of the Consumer Surplus gain against the magnitude of the Producer Surplus loss.
Recall that Total Social Surplus is the sum TS = CS + PS, so net welfare rises whenever Delta CS + Delta PS > 0.

options_template.text: Domestic producers do not lose any surplus when a country imports because foreign firms absorb the price drop.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (No-Loser Illusion): Domestic producers definitely lose Producer Surplus when the domestic price drops from P_A to P_w.

options_template.text: Government tariff revenue automatically offsets any loss suffered by domestic producers under free trade.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Free-Trade Tariff Confusion): Under free trade there is no tariff and therefore zero tariff revenue.

options_template.text: The expansion in domestic Consumer Surplus strictly exceeds the reduction in domestic Producer Surplus, leaving a positive net gain in Total Social Surplus.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When P_w < P_A, consumers capture both the surplus transferred from domestic producers and a new net surplus triangle, so Delta CS + Delta PS > 0 while freed domestic resources can shift to comparative-advantage sectors.

options_template.text: Importing raises the domestic price above P_A, which boosts both Consumer Surplus and Producer Surplus simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price Direction Error): Importing lowers the domestic price from P_A to P_w, helping consumers and hurting import-competing producers.

questions.title: Welfare Distribution in an Exporting Country
questions.prompt_template: When a small open economy opens to free trade in a market where P_w > P_A and becomes an exporter, how do Consumer Surplus (CS), Producer Surplus (PS), and Total Social Surplus (TS) change?

hints.text: First determine whether opening to exports causes the domestic price to rise or fall.
Match the higher domestic price to the welfare direction of domestic buyers versus domestic sellers.

options_template.text: CS increases, PS decreases, and TS decreases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Importing-Exporting Swap & Welfare Error): Exporting raises the domestic price, which helps producers and hurts consumers, and free trade increases TS.

options_template.text: CS decreases, PS increases, and TS increases because the gain in PS strictly exceeds the loss in CS.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Opening to exports raises the domestic price from P_A to P_w, reducing domestic Consumer Surplus but expanding Producer Surplus by a strictly larger amount, yielding Delta TS > 0.

options_template.text: Both CS and PS increase because selling abroad expands domestic production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Universal Winner Fallacy): Domestic consumers must now pay the higher world price P_w instead of P_A, so Consumer Surplus strictly falls.

options_template.text: CS decreases, PS increases by the exact same dollar amount, and TS remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Sum Trade Fallacy): Trade is not zero-sum; producers gain not only the transfer from domestic consumers but also additional surplus from selling exports at P_w above domestic marginal cost.

questions.title: Concentrated Losses vs. Dispersed Gains in Trade Politics
questions.prompt_template: Why do import-competing industries often lobby successfully for tariffs even though free trade increases Total Social Surplus for the nation as a whole?

hints.text: Compare the per-person stake of a steelworker facing import competition versus an individual consumer saving a modest amount on retail goods.
Think about how concentration of benefits or losses affects the incentive to organize politically.

options_template.text: Because the losses from import competition are concentrated among specific domestic firms and workers, while the gains from lower prices are spread thinly across millions of consumers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Concentrated producer losses create intense lobbying incentives, whereas dispersed consumer gains (such as saving $30 on a pair of shoes) give individual households little incentive to organize politically.

options_template.text: Because consumers are legally barred from purchasing imported goods once domestic producers petition the government.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal Ban Misconception): Consumers are not legally barred from buying imports prior to trade policy enactment; the political asymmetry stems from economic incentives.

options_template.text: Because free trade actually lowers Total Social Surplus whenever a country imports manufactured goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mercantilist Fallacy): Free trade increases Total Social Surplus in both importing and exporting markets.

options_template.text: Because domestic producers always outnumber domestic consumers in a small open economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Population Count Error): Consumers vastly outnumber producers in any single industry; producers organize effectively because their per-capita stakes are concentrated, not because they are more numerous.

questions.title: Distinguishing a Tariff from an Import Quota
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately contrasts a tariff with an import quota?

hints.text: Focus on the policy instrument: one acts directly on price via taxation, while the other restricts physical volume.
Also consider whether the policy directly generates government tax revenue.

options_template.text: A tariff caps the physical quantity of imports, whereas an import quota taxes each imported unit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Instrument Reversal): This reverses the two definitions; tariffs are taxes and quotas are physical quantity limits.

options_template.text: A tariff applies only to exported goods, whereas an import quota applies only to imported goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Export-Import Confusion): An import tariff is levied on imported goods entering the country.

options_template.text: A tariff is a per-unit or percentage tax levied on imported goods, whereas an import quota is a legal cap on the physical quantity of imports allowed to enter the country.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A tariff restricts trade by taxing imports (raising price directly and generating tax revenue), whereas a quota restricts trade by placing a statutory ceiling on import volume.

options_template.text: A tariff causes deadweight loss, whereas an import quota eliminates deadweight loss by fixing quantity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quota Efficiency Myth): An import quota restricting imports to the same volume as a tariff creates the exact same production and consumption deadweight loss triangles (B + D).

questions.title: Production Inefficiency vs. Consumption Inefficiency Under a Tariff
questions.prompt_template: In the standard tariff welfare decomposition (Areas A, B, C, and D), what distinct economic inefficiencies do deadweight loss Triangles B and D represent?

hints.text: Look at which side of the market each triangle touches: Triangle B sits under the domestic supply curve, and Triangle D sits under the domestic demand curve.
Connect domestic supply expansion to higher production costs, and domestic demand contraction to lost consumer willingness to pay.

options_template.text: Triangle B represents lost government tariff revenue, and Triangle D represents lost domestic producer surplus.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Region Label Confusion): Government tariff revenue is Rectangle C, and domestic producers actually gain Trapezoid A.

options_template.text: Triangle B represents consumption inefficiency from higher prices, and Triangle D represents production inefficiency from domestic overproduction.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Triangle B-D Reversal): Triangle B is on the supply side (production inefficiency) and Triangle D is on the demand side (consumption inefficiency).

options_template.text: Triangle B represents production inefficiency from using higher-cost domestic resources to produce units that could have been imported at P_w, while Triangle D represents consumption inefficiency from pricing out buyers whose willingness to pay exceeds P_w.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Triangle B wastes productive resources on high-cost domestic output above P_w, and Triangle D destroys surplus from mutually beneficial purchases forgone between P_w and P_w + t.

options_template.text: Both Triangles B and D represent transfers from domestic consumers to foreign exporters.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer vs. Waste Confusion): Deadweight loss is permanently destroyed surplus that accrues to no one—neither domestic nor foreign agents.

questions.title: Why an Import Tariff Creates Two Deadweight Loss Triangles
questions.prompt_template: Why does a per-unit import tariff in a small open economy generate two separate deadweight loss triangles (B and D), unlike a standard domestic excise tax which generates a single Harberger triangle?

hints.text: Compare how a domestic excise tax versus an import tariff affects domestic producers.
Remember that a tariff simultaneously encourages high-cost domestic production and discourages domestic consumption.

options_template.text: Because a tariff distorts both production decisions (pulling higher-cost domestic suppliers into the market above P_w) and consumption decisions (pricing out domestic buyers above P_w).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Raising the domestic price from P_w to P_w + t simultaneously induces inefficient domestic production expansion (Triangle B) and inefficient domestic consumption contraction (Triangle D).

options_template.text: Because a tariff is levied twice—once when the good leaves the foreign port and once when it reaches domestic consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Taxation Myth): A per-unit tariff is collected once at the border; the two triangles arise from dual behavioral distortions on supply and demand.

options_template.text: Because domestic demand is always perfectly inelastic while domestic supply is perfectly elastic.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity Misstatement): If demand were perfectly inelastic, consumption would not fall and Triangle D would equal zero.

options_template.text: Because one triangle measures domestic deadweight loss and the other measures foreign deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Domestic vs. Foreign DWL Confusion): In a small open economy, both Triangles B and D are domestic deadweight losses borne inside the importing country.

questions.title: Quota Rents and Import License Allocation
questions.prompt_template: When a government replaces a per-unit tariff with an equivalent import quota (restricting imports to the exact same volume), what happens to Area C if the import licenses are given away free of charge to foreign exporters (as in a voluntary export restraint)?

hints.text: Recall that Area C equals (P_q - P_w) times the volume of allowed imports.
Ask who receives that per-unit markup when foreign exporters hold the right to sell at the higher domestic price.

options_template.text: Area C is still collected by the domestic treasury as tax revenue, keeping domestic welfare loss at B + D.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic Revenue Fallacy): Quotas do not automatically generate government revenue unless the government auctions the import licenses.

options_template.text: Area C disappears completely, reducing the domestic price back down to P_w.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rent Disappearance Error): Because the quota restricts imports, the domestic price remains at P_w + t, creating valuable quota rents equal to Area C.

options_template.text: Area C transfers to domestic consumers as a rebate, offsetting their surplus loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumer Rebate Error): Domestic consumers still pay the higher domestic price P_w + t and lose A + B + C + D.

options_template.text: Area C becomes quota rents captured by foreign exporters, expanding the importing nation's net welfare loss from B + D to B + C + D.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When foreign exporters hold the quota licenses, they buy or produce at P_w and sell into the protected market at P_w + t, capturing Area C and worsening the importing nation's net loss to B + C + D.

questions.title: The National Security Argument and Its Economic Critique
questions.prompt_template: What is the core economic caution regarding the 'national security' argument for tariffs on sectors such as specialty steel, semiconductors, or aerospace?

hints.text: Consider both the political incentive of domestic industries and alternative ways to ensure emergency supply.
Ask whether border tariffs are the lowest-cost method for securing defense-critical materials.

options_template.text: National security is never a valid concern because foreign supply chains can never be disrupted during geopolitical crises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dismissal of Geopolitical Risk): Economists acknowledge genuine defense-supply vulnerabilities; their critique focuses on overuse of the label and policy efficiency.

options_template.text: Industries frequently stretch the 'national security' label to win protection even when stockpiling, allied sourcing, or direct production subsidies would achieve security at far lower social cost.
options_template.feedback: Correct. While preserving truly defense-critical capacity can be justified, the label is easily abused by lobbying groups, and alternatives like stockpiling or direct subsidies avoid distorting consumer prices.

options_template.text: Tariffs on defense-critical goods always lower domestic prices, which reduces domestic manufacturing capacity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price Direction Error): Tariffs raise domestic prices rather than lowering them.

options_template.text: National security tariffs cannot generate deadweight loss because defense goods have no opportunity cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Opportunity Cost Fallacy): Allocating scarce resources via tariffs still incurs production and consumption deadweight loss.

questions.title: The Infant Industry Argument for Temporary Protection
questions.prompt_template: What economic rationale underlies the 'infant industry' argument for temporary trade protection, and what is its main practical weakness?

hints.text: Think about what young domestic firms need to achieve before they can match established global competitors' unit costs.
Consider the informational and political challenges governments face when granting temporary protection.

options_template.text: Rationale: shielding young firms lets them achieve economies of scale and learning-by-doing; Weakness: governments struggle to pick future winners and 'temporary' tariffs often become politically entrenched.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Infant industry protection aims to bridge early high-cost phases via scale and learning-by-doing, but policymakers rarely out-predict markets and protected firms lobby fiercely to keep tariffs permanent.

options_template.text: Rationale: tariffs permanently lower consumer prices in new sectors; Weakness: domestic firms immediately exit the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Effect Reversal): Tariffs raise consumer prices and attract domestic firms into the protected sector rather than forcing them out.

options_template.text: Rationale: young industries lack comparative advantage forever; Weakness: tariffs generate too much consumer surplus.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Permanent Inefficiency Misstatement): The infant industry argument explicitly presumes the industry will eventually gain comparative advantage, and tariffs reduce rather than increase consumer surplus.

options_template.text: Rationale: tariffs eliminate the need for capital investment; Weakness: foreign countries never have infant industries.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital-Free Growth Error): Achieving economies of scale still requires heavy capital investment; the barrier is transitional cost competitiveness.

questions.title: Dumping and Anti-Dumping Policy
questions.prompt_template: In international trade economics, how is 'dumping' defined, and why do economists view many real-world anti-dumping complaints with skepticism?

hints.text: Focus on the benchmark prices used to define dumping: production cost or home-market price.
Distinguish predatory pricing intended to monopolize a market from legitimate foreign cost efficiency.

options_template.text: Dumping is exporting a product above its home-market price; economists are skeptical because higher export prices hurt domestic producers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price Direction Reversal): Dumping involves selling *below* cost of production or below the home-market price, not above it.

options_template.text: Dumping is importing goods without paying tariffs; economists are skeptical because customs agencies cannot track physical shipments.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Smuggling Conflation): Evading tariffs is smuggling or customs fraud, not economic dumping.

options_template.text: Dumping is exporting a product below its cost of production or below its home-market price; economists are skeptical because anti-dumping complaints are frequently filed against foreign rivals that are simply more efficient.
options_template.feedback: Correct. While anti-dumping tariffs can deter predatory pricing, domestic competitors routinely use anti-dumping petitions to shield themselves from legitimately lower-cost foreign producers.

options_template.text: Dumping is restricting exports through a voluntary export restraint; economists are skeptical because it lowers domestic prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (VER Conflation): Voluntary export restraints restrict supply and raise prices in the importing country, which is the opposite of dumping.

questions.title: WTO, USMCA, and the Tariff-War Prisoner's Dilemma
questions.prompt_template: Why do nations join multilateral institutions like the World Trade Organization (WTO) and regional agreements like the USMCA?

hints.text: Think about what happens when every country unilaterally raises tariffs to protect its own industries.
Connect reciprocal tariff commitments to overcoming a classic game-theoretic dilemma.

options_template.text: To help member nations coordinate simultaneous tariff hikes that maximize global government tax revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue Cartel Misconception): The WTO and USMCA exist to lower trade barriers and resolve disputes, not to coordinate tariff increases.

options_template.text: To avoid destructive tit-for-tat tariff wars—a classic Prisoner's Dilemma in which unilateral protection leaves every trading partner worse off.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Without binding trade agreements, each country faces a political temptation to erect tariffs unilaterally, provoking retaliation that shrinks trade and reduces welfare for all nations.

options_template.text: To guarantee that every member nation maintains an autarky price equal to its world price in all markets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Autarky-Price Equalization Error): Trade agreements promote specialization based on differences between autarky prices and world prices, not autarky.

options_template.text: To replace all domestic production subsidies with import quotas.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Instrument Inversion): Trade agreements generally discourage import quotas and favor transparent rules rather than replacing subsidies with quotas.

questions.title: Identifying Import Volume and Net Gain Triangle on a Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a domestic supply-and-demand diagram for a small open economy where the horizontal world price line P_w lies below the autarky equilibrium price P_A, how are import volume and the net gain in Total Social Surplus (Delta TS) represented geometrically?

hints.text: Trace horizontally along P_w from the domestic supply curve to the domestic demand curve.
Look at the triangle bounded above by the autarky equilibrium point (Q_A, P_A) and below by the world price line P_w.

options_template.text: Imports equal the horizontal segment Q_d(P_w) - Q_s(P_w) along the P_w line, and Delta TS equals the triangle bounded by the domestic supply curve, the domestic demand curve, and the P_w line below the autarky equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P_w < P_A, domestic demand exceeds domestic supply by Q_d - Q_s (imports), and the net social surplus gain is the triangle with base (Q_d - Q_s) and height (P_A - P_w).

options_template.text: Imports equal Q_A - Q_s(P_w), and Delta TS equals the entire area under the demand curve above P_w.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Half-Import & Total-CS Confusion): Imports equal the full gap Q_d(P_w) - Q_s(P_w), not just the domestic production drop, and the entire area under demand above P_w is total CS, not Delta TS.

options_template.text: Imports equal Q_d(P_w), and Delta TS equals the rectangle between P_A and P_w up to Q_A.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Domestic-Output & Transfer Confusion): Domestic firms still supply Q_s(P_w), so imports are Q_d - Q_s; the rectangle up to Q_s is a transfer from producers to consumers, not net social gain.

options_template.text: Imports equal the vertical distance P_A - P_w, and Delta TS equals the area below the supply curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-Swap Error): Quantities (imports) are measured horizontally along the Q-axis, while prices (P_A - P_w) are measured vertically.

questions.title: Identifying Export Volume and Net Gain Triangle on a Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a domestic supply-and-demand diagram where the horizontal world price line P_w lies above the autarky equilibrium price P_A, where is the net gain in Total Social Surplus (Delta TS) located?

hints.text: At P_w > P_A, domestic quantity supplied exceeds domestic quantity demanded.
Identify the region added to Producer Surplus that is NOT merely transferred away from domestic Consumer Surplus.

options_template.text: The trapezoid between P_A and P_w to the left of the domestic demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer Region Confusion): The trapezoid between P_A and P_w to the left of domestic demand is a pure transfer from domestic consumers to domestic producers, netting to zero in Total Social Surplus.

options_template.text: The triangle above the autarky equilibrium bounded by the domestic demand curve, the domestic supply curve, and the horizontal P_w line, with base Q_s(P_w) - Q_d(P_w) and height P_w - P_A.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Domestic producers gain the entire trapezoid between P_A and P_w out to Q_s(P_w), while domestic consumers lose the portion up to the demand curve; the remaining triangle above the autarky point is the net gain Delta TS.

options_template.text: The triangle below P_A bounded by the vertical price axis and the domestic supply curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Autarky PS Confusion): The triangle below P_A above the supply curve is autarky Producer Surplus, not the gain from trade.

options_template.text: The rectangle of height P_w and width Q_d(P_w).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Expenditure Rectangle Error): P_w times Q_d(P_w) is domestic consumer expenditure at the world price, not a welfare gain.

questions.topic: Comparative Statics of World Price Changes
questions.title: Effect of a Further Drop in World Price for an Importing Country
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a small open economy is already importing steel at a world price P_w1 < P_A. If global technological improvements lower the world price further to P_w2 < P_w1 (ceteris paribus), how does the diagram change?

hints.text: Shift the horizontal world price line downward from P_w1 to P_w2 and read the new intersections with domestic supply and demand.
Check how the horizontal gap Q_d - Q_s and the height P_A - P_w respond.

options_template.text: Domestic quantity supplied increases, domestic quantity demanded decreases, imports shrink, and the net gains-from-trade triangle gets smaller.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Response Reversal): Moving down the upward-sloping supply curve reduces Q_s, while moving down the downward-sloping demand curve increases Q_d.

options_template.text: Both domestic demand and domestic supply curves shift to the right, leaving imports unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Movement Confusion): A change in the world price causes movements along the existing domestic supply and demand curves, not shifts of those curves.

options_template.text: Domestic quantity supplied falls, domestic quantity demanded rises, import volume expands, and the net gains-from-trade triangle becomes strictly larger.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A lower P_w moves down along domestic supply (lower Q_s) and down along domestic demand (higher Q_d), widening both the base (imports) and height (P_A - P_w) of the net surplus triangle.

options_template.text: Import volume expands, but Total Social Surplus falls because domestic producer surplus declines further.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Producer-Only Welfare Bias): Although PS falls further, CS rises by an even larger amount, strictly increasing Total Social Surplus.

questions.topic: Comparative Statics of World Price Changes
questions.title: Effect of a Rise in World Price for an Exporting Country
questions.prompt_template: A small open economy exports soybeans at world price P_w1 > P_A. If a surge in global demand pushes the world price up to P_w2 > P_w1, what happens graphically in the domestic soybean market?

hints.text: Move the horizontal world price line upward from P_w1 to P_w2.
Compare the new domestic Q_s and Q_d intersections along the domestic supply and demand curves.

options_template.text: Domestic quantity supplied rises, domestic quantity demanded falls, exports expand, domestic CS falls further, and domestic PS and Total Social Surplus both increase.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher world price moves up along domestic supply (more output) and up along domestic demand (less domestic consumption), expanding export volume and enlarging the net gain triangle above autarky.

options_template.text: Domestic quantity supplied rises and domestic quantity demanded also rises because the country is richer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Law of Demand Violation): Ceteris paribus, a higher domestic price causes a movement upward along the downward-sloping domestic demand curve, reducing Q_d.

options_template.text: Domestic Consumer Surplus expands while Domestic Producer Surplus shrinks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Buyer-Seller Welfare Swap): A higher price hurts domestic buyers (lower CS) and benefits domestic sellers (higher PS).

options_template.text: The domestic supply curve shifts left so that exports remain constant.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Movement Confusion): A higher world price induces a movement along the fixed domestic supply curve rather than shifting it.

questions.topic: Tariff Welfare Diagram (Areas A, B, C, D)
questions.title: Graphical Loss in Consumer Surplus Under a Tariff
questions.prompt_template: In the standard tariff diagram (Figure 14.2) where a per-unit tariff t raises the domestic price from P_w to P_w + t, which combination of labeled areas equals the total loss in domestic Consumer Surplus (Delta CS)?

hints.text: Compare the consumer surplus triangle above P_w with the smaller consumer surplus triangle above P_w + t.
The difference between those two triangles is the horizontal trapezoid stretching from the vertical price axis all the way to the demand curve between P_w and P_w + t.

options_template.text: -(B + D) only, because A and C remain inside the domestic economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Net-Loss vs. Consumer-Loss Confusion): -(B + D) is the net loss to society as a whole; consumers themselves lose all four regions A, B, C, and D.

options_template.text: -(A + B + C + D), representing the entire trapezoid lost between P_w and P_w + t under the domestic demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When the domestic price rises from P_w to P_w + t, Consumer Surplus shrinks by the entire band under the demand curve between those two prices, which is partitioned into A + B + C + D.

options_template.text: -(C + D) only, because consumers only pay the tariff on imported units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Import-Only Price Myth): Domestic producers also raise their price to P_w + t, so consumers pay the higher price on domestically produced units as well (losing A and B in addition to C and D).

options_template.text: -(A + C) only, because triangles B and D do not involve cash payments.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cash-Flow-Only Bias): Consumers also lose surplus on the units they stop buying (Triangle D) and on the higher-cost domestic units (Triangle B), even though no cash changes hands on forgone units.

questions.topic: Tariff Welfare Diagram (Areas A, B, C, D)
questions.title: Geometric Shape of Domestic Producer Surplus Gain Under a Tariff
questions.prompt_template: When a per-unit tariff t raises the domestic price from P_w to P_w + t, why is the gain in domestic Producer Surplus (Area A) a trapezoid rather than a rectangle of width Q_s2?

hints.text: Trace the domestic supply curve between Q_s1 (at P_w) and Q_s2 (at P_w + t).
On the newly added domestic units between Q_s1 and Q_s2, is domestic marginal cost equal to P_w or rising above P_w?

options_template.text: Because the domestic supply curve is upward-sloping, so marginal cost rises above P_w on the extra units between Q_s1 and Q_s2; Area A lies above the supply curve, while Triangle B below it represents extra production cost.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Domestic firms earn the full price hike t on existing output Q_s1 (a rectangle), plus only the triangle above the rising supply curve on the expanded units (Q_s2 - Q_s1), forming Trapezoid A.

options_template.text: Because domestic producers must remit half of their revenue to the government as tariff taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Domestic Tax Confusion): Import tariffs are levied only on imported units, not on domestically produced units.

options_template.text: Because domestic output falls from Q_s2 to Q_s1 when a tariff is imposed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply Response Reversal): A higher domestic price induces domestic producers to expand output from Q_s1 to Q_s2.

options_template.text: Because the world price falls below P_w whenever a small open economy imposes a tariff.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Large-Country Confusion): A small open economy takes P_w as fixed.

questions.topic: Tariff Welfare Diagram (Areas A, B, C, D)
questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Prohibitive Tariff on Area C
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a small open economy sets a per-unit tariff so high that P_w + t equals or exceeds the autarky price P_A (a prohibitive tariff). What happens graphically to imports, tariff revenue (Area C), and deadweight loss (B + D)?

hints.text: At P_A, compare domestic quantity supplied Q_s and domestic quantity demanded Q_d.
If imports drop to zero, calculate the width of Rectangle C and compare the resulting surplus to free trade.

options_template.text: Imports reach their maximum, tariff revenue (Area C) is maximized, and deadweight loss falls to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Prohibitive Revenue Illusion): When a tariff is so high that no imports enter, tax revenue t times 0 equals zero.

options_template.text: Imports fall to zero, tariff revenue (Area C) shrinks to zero, and deadweight loss (B + D) expands to equal the entire free-trade net gains triangle.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A prohibitive tariff pushes the market back to autarky (P_A, Q_A), eliminating all imports and tariff revenue (C = 0) while destroying the entire gains-from-trade triangle.

options_template.text: Imports fall to zero, but tariff revenue (Area C) remains positive because domestic firms pay the tariff.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Domestic Tariff Collection Error): Only imported units are subject to a tariff; with zero imports, tariff revenue is strictly zero.

options_template.text: The domestic price rises above P_A to P_w + t even though domestic supply exceeds domestic demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Above-Autarky Price Error): Competition among domestic producers prevents the domestic price from rising above the autarky market-clearing price P_A.

questions.topic: Tariff Welfare Diagram (Areas A, B, C, D)
questions.title: Reading Marginal Cost Inside Deadweight Loss Triangle B
questions.prompt_template: Consider the units between Q_s1 and Q_s2 along the horizontal axis of a tariff diagram. Why does Triangle B measure a pure waste of economic resources?

hints.text: Compare the height of the domestic supply curve (domestic marginal cost) to the height of the world price line P_w across the interval from Q_s1 to Q_s2.
Remember that the nation could have obtained those same units from abroad at a cost of P_w per unit.

options_template.text: For every unit between Q_s1 and Q_s2, domestic marginal cost lies above the world price P_w, so producing those units domestically uses more resources than importing them at P_w.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The vertical gap between the domestic supply curve and P_w over [Q_s1, Q_s2] measures the excess resource cost of domestic overproduction—literally Triangle B.

options_template.text: For every unit between Q_s1 and Q_s2, domestic marginal cost is below P_w, so domestic firms earn negative profits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply Curve Position Error): Units with domestic marginal cost below P_w are already produced under free trade (from 0 to Q_s1).

options_template.text: Consumers refuse to purchase domestically produced units between Q_s1 and Q_s2, leaving them unsold.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unsold Inventory Myth): Those units are sold at P_w + t; the inefficiency is that they are produced at higher cost than the world price.

options_template.text: The government must pay a subsidy equal to Triangle B to foreign exporters.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Foreign Subsidy Confusion): A tariff does not pay foreign exporters; Triangle B is domestic production inefficiency.

questions.topic: Tariff Welfare Diagram (Areas A, B, C, D)
questions.title: Reading Willingness to Pay Inside Deadweight Loss Triangle D
questions.prompt_template: On a tariff diagram, look at the horizontal interval from Q_d2 to Q_d1 where domestic consumption contracts after a tariff raises price from P_w to P_w + t. What is true for every unit in this interval?

hints.text: Compare the height of the domestic demand curve (willingness to pay) against both P_w and P_w + t.
Check whether society gains if a buyer values a unit more than its world cost P_w.

options_template.text: Buyers' willingness to pay is below P_w, so society is better off not consuming those units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Below-World-Price Error): Units with willingness to pay below P_w were never purchased even under free trade (they lie to the right of Q_d1).

options_template.text: Buyers' willingness to pay exceeds P_w + t, so they continue purchasing those units despite the tariff.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Active-Purchase Confusion): Units with willingness to pay above P_w + t are still purchased (between 0 and Q_d2).

options_template.text: Buyers' willingness to pay lies above the world cost P_w but below the tariff-inflated price P_w + t, so mutually beneficial consumption is priced out of the market.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Every unit between Q_d2 and Q_d1 has marginal benefit above the world price P_w, yet the tariff blocks the transaction—creating consumption deadweight loss Triangle D.

options_template.text: Buyers' willingness to pay equals zero because the tariff shifts the demand curve to the left.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand Shift Confusion): A tariff moves buyers upward along a stationary domestic demand curve; willingness to pay does not drop to zero.

questions.topic: Tariff vs. Equivalent Import Quota Diagram
questions.title: Comparing an Import Quota to a Tariff on the Same Graph
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a government replaces a $10 per-unit steel tariff (which reduced imports from 20 tons to 10 tons and raised domestic price from $40 to $50) with a strict 10-ton import quota. How do the graphical quantities Q_s2, Q_d2, and the domestic price compare?

hints.text: Find the unique domestic price at which the horizontal gap Q_d(P) - Q_s(P) equals the 10-ton quota limit.
Recall Table 14.2's equivalence between a tariff and a quota restricting imports to the same volume.

options_template.text: The domestic price stays at $40 because no tax is collected at the border.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Tax Price Fallacy): Restricting imports to 10 tons creates a shortage at $40, bidding the domestic price up to $50 until Q_d - Q_s = 10.

options_template.text: The domestic price rises to $50, domestic supply expands to Q_s2, domestic demand contracts to Q_d2, and Areas A, B, C, and D have the exact same geometric sizes—except Area C becomes quota rents rather than tax revenue.
options_template.feedback: Correct. An import quota set equal to post-tariff import volume reproduces the exact same domestic price ($50), quantities, and triangles B and D; only the recipient of Area C changes.

options_template.text: Domestic supply remains frozen at free-trade Q_s1 while domestic demand absorbs the entire 10-ton cut.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frozen-Supply Error): As the domestic price rises to $50, domestic producers move up their supply curve from Q_s1 to Q_s2.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss doubles because quotas eliminate both domestic supply and domestic demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-DWL Myth): If import licenses are held domestically, total deadweight loss is identical (B + D); only foreign license capture adds Area C to domestic welfare loss.

questions.topic: Comparative Statics: Tariff vs. Quota Under Demand Shift
questions.title: Outward Demand Shift Under a Tariff vs. Under a Binding Quota
questions.prompt_template: In a small open economy, suppose domestic demand for steel shifts rightward (increases) due to a construction boom. How does the domestic price response differ graphically under a fixed per-unit tariff (t) compared to a fixed binding import quota?

hints.text: Under a fixed per-unit tariff in a small open economy, foreign supply remains perfectly elastic at P_w + t.
Under a fixed quota, imports cannot expand when demand shifts right, so the domestic market must clear through price.

options_template.text: Under a fixed tariff, the domestic price remains anchored at P_w + t and imports expand to meet the extra demand; under a fixed quota, imports cannot rise, so the domestic price climbs even higher.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A tariff keeps the domestic price capped at P_w + t while allowing import volume to absorb demand growth, whereas a fixed physical quota forces the domestic price upward when demand shifts right.

options_template.text: Under a fixed tariff, the domestic price rises sharply; under a fixed quota, the domestic price stays fixed because import volume is regulated.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tariff-Quota Mechanism Reversal): A tariff fixes the price wedge above P_w (letting quantity adjust), whereas a quota fixes import quantity (forcing price to adjust).

options_template.text: Under both policies, the domestic price stays unchanged and domestic producers supply all of the new demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Horizontal Domestic Supply Error): Domestic supply is upward-sloping, so domestic producers will only supply more if the domestic price rises.

options_template.text: Under both policies, the domestic price falls because higher demand creates economies of scale.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Shift Price Reversal): A rightward shift in demand never lowers price along an upward-sloping supply curve or fixed price line.

questions.topic: Targeting Principle: Subsidy vs. Tariff Diagram
questions.title: Graphical Deadweight Loss: Production Subsidy vs. Import Tariff
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 14.3 and the Targeting Principle analysis, why does a $10 per-ton domestic production subsidy achieve the same +5-ton expansion in domestic steel output as a $10 per-ton import tariff while cutting deadweight loss in half?

hints.text: Compare the price domestic consumers pay under a $10 tariff ($50) versus under a $10 domestic production subsidy ($40).
Check which of the two deadweight loss triangles (B or D) disappears when consumers still face P_w.

options_template.text: The subsidy eliminates production inefficiency (Triangle B) while keeping consumption inefficiency (Triangle D).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Triangle B-D Swap): Expanding higher-cost domestic output from 10 to 15 tons still incurs production inefficiency (Triangle B); it is consumption inefficiency (Triangle D) that disappears.

options_template.text: The subsidy raises domestic producer price to P_w + s (incurring Triangle B) while leaving the consumer price unchanged at P_w, thereby completely eliminating consumption deadweight loss (Triangle D).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because domestic buyers still pay P_w and purchase Q_d1, no consumption distortion occurs (D = 0), leaving only production deadweight loss Triangle B.

options_template.text: The subsidy eliminates both Triangle B and Triangle D, resulting in zero deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Costless-Subsidy Fallacy): Expanding domestic production along an upward-sloping supply curve above P_w still wastes real resources equal to Triangle B.

options_template.text: The subsidy shifts the world price downward by $10, transferring the cost to foreign suppliers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Small-Country Price Error): A small open economy cannot alter the world price P_w.

questions.title: Effect of Flatter Domestic Demand on Consumption Deadweight Loss
questions.prompt_template: Holding the world price P_w, the per-unit tariff t, and the initial free-trade consumption Q_d1 constant, how does a flatter (more price-elastic) domestic demand curve affect consumption deadweight loss Triangle D?

hints.text: Recall that Triangle D = (1/2) * t * (Q_d1 - Q_d2).
Ask whether a flatter demand curve produces a larger or smaller drop in quantity demanded (Q_d1 - Q_d2) for the same price increase t.

options_template.text: Triangle D becomes smaller because buyers are less responsive to the tariff price hike.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Elasticity Inversion): A flatter demand curve through a given point is *more* responsive (more elastic) to price changes, not less.

options_template.text: Triangle D becomes larger because the same price increase t causes a larger contraction in domestic quantity demanded (Q_d1 - Q_d2).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because Triangle D has height t and base (Q_d1 - Q_d2), a flatter (more elastic) demand curve generates a larger drop in quantity demanded and therefore a larger consumption deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Triangle D is unaffected because deadweight loss depends only on the size of the tariff t.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Quantity Fallacy): Deadweight loss depends on both the tariff height t and the behavioral quantity distortion (Q_d1 - Q_d2).

options_template.text: Triangle D turns into tariff revenue Rectangle C.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lost-Sales Revenue Error): Units that consumers stop buying generate zero tariff revenue; greater demand contraction actually shrinks tariff revenue Rectangle C.

questions.title: Calculating Autarky Equilibrium and Total Social Surplus
questions.prompt_template: In a small open economy, domestic inverse demand for aluminum is P = 120 - 3Q_d and domestic inverse supply is P = 20 + 2Q_s, where P is in dollars per ton and Q is in tons. Before the country opens to trade (autarky), what is Total Social Surplus (TS_A)?

hints.text: First find the autarky equilibrium (Q_A, P_A) by setting inverse demand equal to inverse supply.
Use the vertical intercepts ($120 for demand, $20 for supply) to compute CS_A = 0.5 * Q_A * (120 - P_A) and PS_A = 0.5 * Q_A * (P_A - 20), then sum them.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumer-Surplus-Only Error): $600 is only autarky Consumer Surplus (0.5 * 20 * 60); you must add Producer Surplus ($400) to obtain Total Social Surplus.
Diagnostic fallacy (Producer-Surplus-Only Error): $400 is only autarky Producer Surplus (0.5 * 20 * 40); Total Social Surplus equals CS_A + PS_A.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Triangle Factor): Multiplying Q_A * (120 - 20) = 20 * 100 = $2,000 omits the 1/2 factor required for triangle areas.

questions.title: Computing Imports and Net Social Surplus Gain
questions.prompt_template: Domestic inverse demand for steel is P = 100 - 2Q_d and domestic inverse supply is P = 20 + 2Q_s (autarky equilibrium: P_A = $60, Q_A = 20 tons). If the country opens to free trade at a world price of P_w = $30 per ton, what is the net gain in Total Social Surplus (Delta TS)?

hints.text: Substitute P_w = $30 into both inverse equations to find Q_s, Q_d, and Imports = Q_d - Q_s.
Apply the gains-from-trade triangle formula: Delta TS = (1/2) * Imports * (P_A - P_w).

options_template.feedback: Correct. At P_w = $30, Q_s = (30 - 20)/2 = 5 tons and Q_d = (100 - 30)/2 = 35 tons, so Imports = 35 - 5 = 30 tons. Thus Delta TS = 0.5 * 30 * ($60 - $30) = $450.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Triangle Factor): Multiplying Imports * (P_A - P_w) = 30 * $30 = $900 forgets the 1/2 factor for a triangle's area.
Diagnostic fallacy (Autarky-Quantity Substitution): Using Q_A = 20 instead of Imports = 30 gives 0.5 * 20 * $30 = $300, understating the trade gain.
Diagnostic fallacy (Domestic-Supply-Only Substitution): Using Q_s = 5 instead of Imports = 30 gives 0.5 * 5 * $30 = $75.

questions.title: Calculating the Change in Consumer Surplus from Free Trade
questions.prompt_template: In a small open economy's market for copper, domestic inverse demand is P = 90 - Q_d and domestic inverse supply is P = 10 + Q_s. Under autarky, P_A = $50 and Q_A = 40 tons. If the country opens to free trade at a world price of P_w = $30 per ton, what is the change in domestic Consumer Surplus (Delta CS)?

hints.text: Compute autarky Consumer Surplus (CS_A) at P_A = $50 and free-trade Consumer Surplus (CS_trade) at P_w = $30.
Subtract CS_A from CS_trade (or compute the trapezoid area 0.5 * (Q_A + Q_d) * (P_A - P_w)).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total vs. Change Confusion): $1,800 is the *total* free-trade Consumer Surplus (0.5 * 60 * 60), not the *change* from autarky CS_A = $800.

Diagnostic fallacy (Rectangle-Only Approximation): Multiplying Q_A * (P_A - P_w) = 40 * $20 = $800 captures only the lower price on existing autarky units and omits the surplus on the 20 newly purchased units.
Diagnostic fallacy (New-Units-Only Error): Computing 0.5 * (60 - 40) * ($50 - $30) = $200 counts only the extra consumption triangle and ignores the $800 savings on the first 40 units.

questions.title: Computing Exports and Net Social Surplus Gain
questions.prompt_template: In a small open economy's wheat market, domestic inverse demand is P = 140 - 2Q_d and domestic inverse supply is P = 20 + 2Q_s (autarky equilibrium: P_A = $80, Q_A = 30 tons). If the world price is P_w = $100 per ton, what are the export volume and the net gain in Total Social Surplus (Delta TS)?

hints.text: Since P_w = $100 > P_A = $80, the country exports Exports = Q_s(100) - Q_d(100).
Then compute Delta TS = (1/2) * Exports * (P_w - P_A).

options_template.text: Exports = 20 tons; Delta TS = +$400
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Triangle Factor): Exports are correctly 20 tons, but 20 * ($100 - $80) = $400 omits the 1/2 triangle factor.

options_template.text: Exports = 40 tons; Delta TS = +$400
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total Output as Exports Error): 40 tons is total domestic supply Q_s(100); you must subtract domestic consumption Q_d(100) = 20 tons to find exports.

options_template.text: Exports = 10 tons; Delta TS = +$100
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Half-Gap Calculation Error): Q_s - Q_A = 10 tons counts only the output expansion and ignores the 10-ton drop in domestic consumption that is also exported.

options_template.text: Exports = 20 tons; Delta TS = +$200
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P_w = $100, Q_s = (100 - 20)/2 = 40 tons and Q_d = (140 - 100)/2 = 20 tons, giving Exports = 40 - 20 = 20 tons and Delta TS = 0.5 * 20 * ($100 - $80) = +$200.

questions.title: Calculating the Change in Producer Surplus for an Exporter
questions.prompt_template: Domestic inverse demand for lumber is P = 100 - Q_d and domestic inverse supply is P = 20 + Q_s (autarky equilibrium: P_A = $60, Q_A = 40 units). When the country opens to free trade at a world price of P_w = $70 per unit, what is the change in domestic Producer Surplus (Delta PS)?

hints.text: Compute autarky Producer Surplus at P_A = $60 and free-trade Producer Surplus at P_w = $70.
Subtract PS_A from PS_trade (or compute the trapezoid area 0.5 * (Q_A + Q_s) * (P_w - P_A)).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total vs. Change Confusion): $1,250 is total Producer Surplus under trade; subtracting autarky PS_A = $800 yields +$450.
Diagnostic fallacy (Autarky-Rectangle Error): Q_A * (P_w - P_A) = 40 * $10 = $400 omits the $50 surplus earned on the 10 extra units produced for export.
Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Rectangle Overstatement): Q_s * (P_w - P_A) = 50 * $10 = $500 ignores the rising domestic marginal cost on the additional 10 units.

questions.title: Computing Government Tariff Revenue (Area C)
questions.prompt_template: In a small open economy, domestic inverse demand is P = 120 - 2Q_d, domestic inverse supply is P = 20 + 2Q_s, and the world price is P_w = $40. If the government imposes a per-unit tariff of t = $10 (raising the domestic price to P_t = $50), how much tariff revenue (Area C) does the government collect?

hints.text: Find post-tariff domestic supply Q_s2 and domestic demand Q_d2 at P_t = $50.
Multiply the per-unit tariff t by post-tariff imports (Q_d2 - Q_s2).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Tariff Import Volume Error): Multiplying $10 by pre-tariff imports (40 - 10 = 30) ignores that the tariff shrinks import volume to 20 units.
Correct. At P_t = $50, Q_s2 = (50 - 20)/2 = 15 and Q_d2 = (120 - 50)/2 = 35, so post-tariff imports equal 35 - 15 = 20 units. Tariff revenue C = $10 * 20 = $200.
Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Demand Tax Base Error): Multiplying $10 * Q_d2 = $10 * 35 = $350 mistakenly taxes domestically produced units as well as imports.
Diagnostic fallacy (Domestic-Supply Tax Base Error): Multiplying $10 * Q_s2 = $10 * 15 = $150 uses domestic output instead of post-tariff imports.

questions.title: Calculating Producer Surplus Gain Under a Tariff (Trapezoid A)
questions.prompt_template: In a steel market with domestic inverse demand P = 100 - 2Q_d, domestic inverse supply P = 20 + 2Q_s, and world price P_w = $30, the government levies a per-unit tariff of t = $12 (so P_t = $42). What is the gain in domestic Producer Surplus (Area A)?

hints.text: Compute domestic quantity supplied before the tariff (Q_s1 at $30) and after the tariff (Q_s2 at $42).
Use the trapezoid formula: Area A = ((Q_s1 + Q_s2) / 2) * t.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Post-Tariff Rectangle Overstatement): Computing Q_s2 * t = 11 * $12 = $132 mistakenly includes Triangle B (extra production cost) inside Producer Surplus.
Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Tariff Rectangle Understatement): Computing Q_s1 * t = 5 * $12 = $60 omits the producer surplus earned on the 6 newly added domestic units.
Diagnostic fallacy (Triangle-Only Error): Computing 0.5 * (11 - 5) * $12 = $36 measures only the incremental triangle (or Triangle B) and omits the $60 gain on the initial 5 units.

questions.title: Computing Total Deadweight Loss (B + D) with Asymmetric Slopes
questions.prompt_template: Consider a small open economy where domestic inverse demand is P = 100 - Q_d and domestic inverse supply is P = 20 + 3Q_s. The world price is P_w = $32, and the government imposes a per-unit tariff of t = $12 (raising the domestic price to P_t = $44). What is the total deadweight loss (B + D) of this tariff?

hints.text: Find Q_s1, Q_d1 at P_w = $32 and Q_s2, Q_d2 at P_t = $44.
Calculate Triangle B = 0.5 * t * (Q_s2 - Q_s1) and Triangle D = 0.5 * t * (Q_d1 - Q_d2) separately, then add them.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Production-DWL-Only Error): $24 is only Triangle B = 0.5 * 12 * (8 - 4); you must also add consumption deadweight loss Triangle D = $72.
Diagnostic fallacy (Consumption-DWL-Only Error): $72 is only Triangle D = 0.5 * 12 * (68 - 56); you must also add production deadweight loss Triangle B = $24.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Triangle Factor): Adding 12*(8 - 4) + 12*(68 - 56) = 48 + 144 = $192 omits the 1/2 factor for both triangles.

questions.title: Summing Areas A, B, C, and D to Find Consumer Surplus Loss
questions.prompt_template: In an importing market with linear domestic curves, the world price is P_w = $50. A per-unit tariff of t = $10 raises the domestic price to $60, causing domestic quantity supplied to rise from Q_s1 = 12 to Q_s2 = 18 and domestic quantity demanded to fall from Q_d1 = 40 to Q_d2 = 34. What is the total change in domestic Consumer Surplus (Delta CS)?

hints.text: Compute Areas A, B, C, and D individually using the tariff height t = $10 and the four given quantities.
Cross-check your sum -(A + B + C + D) using the consumer-loss trapezoid formula: -0.5 * (Q_d1 + Q_d2) * t.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Tariff Rectangle Overstatement): Computing -Q_d1 * t = -40 * $10 = -$400 overstates the loss on the 6 forgone units by treating Triangle D as a full rectangle.
Diagnostic fallacy (Post-Tariff Rectangle Understatement): Computing -Q_d2 * t = -34 * $10 = -$340 omits consumption deadweight loss Triangle D (-$30).
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Producer Transfer): Summing only -(B + C + D) = -$220 forgets that consumers also lose Trapezoid A (-$150) transferred to domestic producers.

questions.topic: Import Quota with Foreign License Holders
questions.title: Net Domestic Welfare Loss Under a Foreign-Allocated Import Quota
questions.prompt_template: Domestic inverse demand is P = 120 - 2Q_d, domestic inverse supply is P = 20 + 2Q_s, and the world price is P_w = $40 (so free-trade Q_s1 = 10, Q_d1 = 40, and imports = 30 tons). The government imposes a 20-ton import quota, which raises the domestic price to $50 (Q_s2 = 15, Q_d2 = 35), and allocates all import licenses free of charge to foreign exporters. What is the importing country's net domestic welfare loss?

hints.text: Compute Triangles B and D plus the quota-rent rectangle Area C.
Because foreign exporters capture Area C, include C alongside B and D in the domestic welfare loss.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Domestic-Revenue Assumption): $50 equals B + D ($25 + $25), which would be the domestic loss under a tariff or domestically held licenses, ignoring the $200 quota rent lost abroad.
Diagnostic fallacy (Quota-Rent-Only Error): $200 is only Area C (20 tons * $10); you must also add deadweight loss Triangles B ($25) and D ($25).
Correct. B = 0.5(15 - 10)($10) = $25, D = 0.5(40 - 35)($10) = $25, and foreign-captured quota rents C = 20 * $10 = $200. Total domestic welfare loss = B + C + D = $25 + $200 + $25 = $250.
Diagnostic fallacy (Gross Consumer Loss Confusion): $375 equals A + B + C + D, which ignores that Area A ($125) stays inside the country as domestic Producer Surplus.

questions.title: Calculating Consumer Cost and Deadweight Loss per Job Protected
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a tariff on imported machinery reduces domestic Consumer Surplus by $480,000, increases domestic Producer Surplus by $200,000, generates $180,000 in tariff revenue, and creates $100,000 in deadweight loss while preserving 8 domestic manufacturing jobs. What are the consumer cost per job protected and the deadweight loss per job protected?

hints.text: Use the Chapter 14.3 policy evaluation ratios: divide |Delta CS| by jobs protected, and divide DWL by jobs protected.
Notice that $200,000 + $180,000 + $100,000 = $480,000, confirming the welfare decomposition.

options_template.text: Consumer cost = $25,000 per job; DWL = $12,500 per job
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Producer-Gain vs. Consumer-Cost Swap): $25,000 per job ($200,000 / 8) is the domestic producer surplus gain per job, not the consumer cost per job.

options_template.text: Consumer cost = $60,000 per job; DWL = $22,500 per job
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-as-DWL Confusion): $22,500 per job ($180,000 / 8) is tariff revenue per job, not deadweight loss per job.

options_template.text: Consumer cost = $60,000 per job; DWL = $12,500 per job
options_template.feedback: Correct. Consumer cost per job protected = $480,000 / 8 = $60,000, and deadweight loss per job protected = $100,000 / 8 = $12,500.

options_template.text: Consumer cost = $35,000 per job; DWL = $12,500 per job
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Net-of-Producer-Gain Error): Subtracting producer surplus gain before dividing (($480,000 - $200,000)/8 = $35,000) understates what consumers themselves pay per job.

questions.title: Deadweight Loss of a Production Subsidy vs. an Equivalent Tariff
questions.prompt_template: In the steel market (P = 100 - 2Q_d, P = 20 + 2Q_s, P_w = $40), free-trade domestic output is Q_s1 = 10 tons and domestic demand is Q_d1 = 30 tons. Policymakers want to expand domestic output to Q_s2 = 18 tons (where domestic supply price is $56). Compare the deadweight loss of a $16 per-ton domestic production subsidy against a $16 per-ton import tariff.

hints.text: Under the $16 subsidy, domestic firms receive $56 (producing 18 tons) while consumers still pay $40 (so Triangle D = $0).
Compute Triangle B = 0.5 * (18 - 10) * $16, and for the $16 tariff also compute Triangle D = 0.5 * (30 - Q_d2) * $16 where Q_d2 = (100 - 56)/2 = 22.

options_template.text: Subsidy DWL = $128; Tariff DWL = $64
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Efficiency Reversal): The subsidy avoids consumption distortion Triangle D, so its deadweight loss is strictly smaller than the tariff's, not larger.

options_template.text: Subsidy DWL = $288; Tariff DWL = $128
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fiscal-Outlay-as-DWL Confusion): $288 ($16 * 18) is total government subsidy expenditure; $224 of that transfers to domestic producers as Area A, leaving only $64 as deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Subsidy DWL = $0; Tariff DWL = $128
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Distortion Subsidy Myth): Even a production subsidy induces high-cost domestic output between 10 and 18 tons above P_w, creating production deadweight loss Triangle B = $64.

options_template.text: Subsidy DWL = $64; Tariff DWL = $128
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under the $16 subsidy, DWL = Triangle B = 0.5(18 - 10)($16) = $64 (check: gov cost $288 minus Delta PS $224 = $64). Under the $16 tariff, Q_d2 = 22, adding Triangle D = 0.5(30 - 22)($16) = $64 for total DWL = $128.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Intermediate Input Tariffs and Downstream Industries
questions.title: Bring It Home: Why Automakers Oppose Steel Tariffs
questions.prompt_template: When a country imposes a tariff on imported steel—an intermediate input used in vehicles, appliances, and construction—why do domestic automakers and construction firms strongly oppose the tariff alongside household consumers?

hints.text: Trace how a higher domestic price of steel affects the marginal production costs of steel-using industries.
Consider both profit margins and the international competitiveness of downstream domestic manufacturers.

options_template.text: Because the steel tariff raises the domestic price of steel above P_w, acting as an input-cost tax that squeezes downstream manufacturers' margins, raises retail prices, and weakens their competitiveness against foreign rivals paying P_w.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Domestic steel mills capture Area A, while downstream industries like automakers and construction firms face higher input costs, reduced competitiveness, and potential job losses.

options_template.text: Because steel tariffs legally prohibit domestic automakers from buying steel produced by domestic mills.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Purchasing-Ban Myth): Automakers can buy domestic steel, but domestic mills raise their prices up to P_w + t alongside taxed imports.

options_template.text: Because steel tariffs lower the domestic price of steel, reducing the resale value of existing cars.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Direction Error): Import tariffs raise, rather than lower, the domestic price of steel.

options_template.text: Because downstream manufacturers must directly pay the tariff revenue even when they use zero steel.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unrelated Tax Incidence Error): Downstream firms are harmed through higher input prices for steel and steel-intensive components.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Consumers Pay Far More per Protected Job Than Producers Gain
questions.prompt_template: In Work It Out 14.3, a steel tariff costs domestic consumers $55,000 per protected steelworker job, yet domestic steel producers capture only $25,000 per job in Producer Surplus. Where does the remaining $30,000 per job go?

hints.text: Recall the four-part decomposition of consumer loss: |Delta CS| = A + B + C + D.
Distinguish what goes to domestic producers (A), what goes to the government (C), and what vanishes permanently (B + D).

options_template.text: It is paid directly to domestic automakers as compensation for higher steel prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic Compensation Myth): Standard tariffs do not compensate downstream buyers; those buyers bear part of the consumer loss.

options_template.text: $20,000 per job goes to government tariff revenue (Area C) and $10,000 per job is permanently destroyed as production and consumption deadweight loss (Areas B + D).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Out of $275,000 in consumer losses across 5 protected jobs, $125,000 ($25,000/job) reaches domestic producers, $100,000 ($20,000/job) becomes tariff revenue, and $50,000 ($10,000/job) vanishes as deadweight loss.

options_template.text: All $30,000 per job is paid to foreign steel exporters as higher world prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Small-Country Terms-of-Trade Error): In a small open economy, the world price P_w is unchanged; under a tariff, Area C goes to the domestic treasury, not foreign exporters.

options_template.text: It represents accounting depreciation on idle foreign steel mills.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Foreign-Asset Accounting Error): Areas B, C, and D are domestic welfare transfers and deadweight losses inside the importing nation.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Foreign Exporters Sometimes Prefer a VER Over a Tariff
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an importing country threatens to restrict foreign auto imports by 100,000 vehicles. Why might foreign automakers prefer negotiating a Voluntary Export Restraint (VER) limiting their exports to that volume rather than facing an equivalent import tariff?

hints.text: Compare who captures Area C under an import tariff versus under a VER where foreign exporters control the export licenses.
Remember that both policies raise the importing country's domestic price to the same level P_w + t.

options_template.text: Because a VER allows foreign automakers to keep exporting unlimited vehicles at P_w.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unbinding-VER Error): A VER caps export volume at the exact same reduced quantity as the equivalent tariff.

options_template.text: Because under a VER, foreign exporters capture the quota rents (Area C) by selling their restricted volume at the higher domestic price P_w + t, whereas under a tariff the importing government collects Area C.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A VER transfers Area C from the importing nation's treasury to foreign exporters as windfall quota rents, making the restriction far more profitable for foreign firms and costlier for the importing nation.

options_template.text: Because a VER lowers the domestic price in the importing country, increasing foreign market share.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Direction Error): Restricting supply via a VER raises the domestic price in the importing country.

options_template.text: Because a VER eliminates all deadweight loss triangles B and D in the importing country.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (VER Efficiency Myth): A VER causes the same B + D deadweight loss and adds Area C to the importing nation's net welfare loss.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: The Targeting Principle in Trade Policy
questions.title: Applying the Targeting Principle to Defense-Critical Semiconductors
questions.prompt_template: Suppose lawmakers decide on national security grounds that domestic semiconductor output must expand from 10 million to 15 million chips per year. According to the Targeting Principle, why do economists recommend a direct domestic production subsidy over a border tariff?

hints.text: Ask what the actual policy objective is: expanding domestic production, or discouraging domestic consumption.
Compare the welfare distortions created by a policy that acts directly on domestic producers versus one that raises consumer prices.

options_template.text: A production subsidy directly targets the domestic output goal without raising the price paid by domestic buyers and downstream tech firms, avoiding consumption deadweight loss (Triangle D).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because a production subsidy leaves domestic consumer price at P_w, it achieves the exact same output expansion while eliminating Triangle D and strictly lowering total social deadweight loss.

options_template.text: A production subsidy requires zero government funding, whereas a tariff drains the government budget.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fiscal-Sign Reversal): A subsidy requires government expenditure while a tariff raises government revenue; the subsidy's welfare advantage comes from avoiding consumption distortion Triangle D, not from being fiscally free.

options_template.text: A production subsidy guarantees that domestic semiconductor firms have a comparative advantage at world price P_w.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Comparative-Advantage Illusion): Needing a subsidy to expand output implies domestic marginal cost still exceeds P_w, which is why Triangle B remains positive.

options_template.text: A production subsidy eliminates imports completely while keeping consumer prices at P_w.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Import Error): Domestic consumers continue buying Q_d1 at P_w, so the remaining gap Q_d1 - Q_s2 is still imported.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Diagnosing Policy Failure in Infant Industry Protection
questions.prompt_template: A developing nation imposes a 25% tariff on imported electric batteries, promising to remove the tariff in five years once domestic startups achieve economies of scale. Fifteen years later, domestic producers still cannot match the world price and lobby successfully to keep the tariff indefinitely. Which economic critique of the infant industry argument does this illustrate?

hints.text: Connect the outcome to both informational limits ('picking winners') and political-economy incentives.
Think about whether protected firms have a strong incentive to cut costs once tariffs insulate them from competition.

options_template.text: Governments struggle to pick future global winners in advance, and 'temporary' tariffs frequently become politically entrenched while insulating inefficient firms from competitive pressure.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Real-world infant industry protection often fails because policymakers lack the information to identify viable future winners and protected firms build political coalitions to make temporary barriers permanent.

options_template.text: Economies of scale are theoretically impossible in manufacturing industries.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Anti-Scale Overstatement): Economies of scale and learning-by-doing are real; the critique is about government selection and political entrenchment.

options_template.text: Tariffs automatically force domestic startups to exit before five years have passed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Exit-Effect Reversal): Tariffs raise domestic prices and shield domestic startups from exit rather than forcing them out.

options_template.text: Infant industry tariffs violate the small open economy assumption by immediately raising the world price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (World-Price Error): A small developing country's tariff raises its own domestic price, not the global price.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Stockpiling and Allied Sourcing vs. Permanent Tariffs
questions.prompt_template: Domestic producers of standard commodity fasteners lobby for permanent 30% tariffs, arguing that fasteners are used in military vehicles and therefore qualify for national security protection. What is the strongest economic policy response?

hints.text: Evaluate whether every input used in a defense product requires permanent domestic self-sufficiency via tariffs.
Compare the cost of permanent economy-wide tariffs against strategic stockpiling or sourcing from reliable allies.

options_template.text: Grant the 30% tariff immediately because any product touched by the military has zero deadweight loss when protected.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Blanket Security Fallacy): Tariffs on common commodities still impose heavy consumer losses and deadweight loss across the civilian economy.

options_template.text: Reject permanent broad tariffs and, if a genuine supply-disruption risk exists, use lower-cost targeted measures such as strategic stockpiling or diversified sourcing from allied nations.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Economists warn that industries routinely stretch the national security label; for standard inputs, stockpiling or allied sourcing secures defense readiness without taxing civilian consumers permanently.

options_template.text: Impose an import quota with foreign license holders instead of a tariff to maximize domestic welfare.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Foreign-Quota Error): Giving quota rents to foreign exporters increases domestic welfare loss from B + D to B + C + D.

options_template.text: Ban all exports of military vehicles so that domestic fastener demand falls to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Export-Ban Non-Sequitur): Banning exports harms comparative-advantage industries without addressing input security.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Distinguishing Predatory Dumping from Foreign Comparative Advantage
questions.prompt_template: A foreign solar-panel manufacturer exports panels to a small open economy at a price well below domestic producers' average cost, thanks to lower local energy costs and larger-scale factories. Domestic manufacturers file an anti-dumping petition demanding high tariffs. How should an economist evaluate this claim?

hints.text: Check whether the foreign firm is selling below its *own* production cost (or home-market price), or simply below *domestic* firms' higher costs.
Consider who benefits if the low import price reflects genuine foreign comparative advantage.

options_template.text: Any time a foreign firm undercuts domestic producers' average cost, it constitutes predatory dumping and justifies permanent tariffs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Domestic-Cost Benchmark Error): Selling below *domestic* firms' costs is the essence of foreign comparative advantage, not dumping.

options_template.text: If the foreign firm's low price reflects lower production costs and scale efficiency rather than pricing below its own cost or home price, it is comparative advantage—not dumping—and imposing tariffs would harm domestic consumers and solar installers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Genuine dumping means pricing below the exporter's own cost or home-market price; penalizing legitimately more efficient foreign rivals destroys consumer surplus and raises costs for downstream rooftop solar installers.

options_template.text: Even if the foreign firm is genuinely more efficient, domestic Total Social Surplus falls whenever imports exceed domestic output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Import-Harm Fallacy): Greater foreign efficiency (a lower P_w) strictly expands the importing nation's Total Social Surplus.

options_template.text: Anti-dumping tariffs only affect foreign firms and never raise prices for domestic buyers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Domestic Incidence Myth): In a small open economy, an anti-dumping tariff raises the domestic price by the full tariff amount, directly burdening domestic buyers.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Import Barriers Do Not Raise Net Economy-Wide Employment
questions.prompt_template: A policymaker argues that imposing broad tariffs on imported industrial components will raise total national employment by saving jobs in domestic component factories. Why do economists challenge this claim?
