hints.text: Look beyond the protected industry to downstream manufacturers and export-oriented sectors.
Consider how higher input prices and potential foreign retaliation affect jobs elsewhere in the economy.

options_template.text: Because tariffs never save any jobs even inside the directly protected factory.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Partial-Equilibrium Denial): Tariffs can preserve visible jobs inside the protected industry by expanding domestic output from Q_s1 to Q_s2; the issue is the offsetting job losses elsewhere.

options_template.text: Because higher prices for protected inputs raise costs and cut employment in downstream industries, while reduced household purchasing power and foreign retaliation shrink employment in export-oriented sectors.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Protection shifts labor toward less-efficient import-competing factories at the expense of downstream users and comparative-advantage exporters, failing to raise net economy-wide employment.

options_template.text: Because domestic firms respond to higher tariff-protected prices by cutting output and laying off workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Response Reversal): Higher domestic prices induce protected firms to expand output (from Q_s1 to Q_s2), not contract it.

options_template.text: Because tariffs reduce government tax revenue to zero, forcing immediate public-sector layoffs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Revenue Error): Non-prohibitive tariffs raise positive government revenue (Area C).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Trade Wars as a Prisoner's Dilemma
questions.prompt_template: Two major trading partners currently practice free trade. Each government is tempted to impose unilateral tariffs to protect domestic producers and capture political support, knowing the other nation may retaliate with counter-tariffs. Why does this scenario mirror a classic Prisoner's Dilemma?

hints.text: Compare the payoff of mutual free trade against the payoff of mutual protection (a tit-for-tat tariff war).
Think about how unilateral incentives lead both nations into an outcome where both are worse off.

options_template.text: Each nation has a unilateral temptation to protect its own industries, yet when both impose retaliatory tariffs, trade collapses and both nations end up with lower national welfare than under mutual free trade.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Just as in a Prisoner's Dilemma, unilateral defection (imposing tariffs) provokes retaliation, trapping both nations in a mutually destructive tariff war—which is why binding WTO/USMCA commitments are valuable.

options_template.text: Both nations maximize their combined Total Social Surplus when both raise tariffs simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mutual-Protection Gain Myth): Mutual tariffs destroy comparative-advantage gains and impose deadweight losses in both countries.

options_template.text: Neither nation has any political incentive to impose tariffs, so trade wars never occur in practice.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Incentive Misstatement): Concentrated domestic lobbying creates strong unilateral incentives to protect, making cooperative trade agreements necessary.

options_template.text: Retaliatory tariffs only harm the country that moves first, leaving the retaliating country unaffected.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Costless-Retaliation Myth): A country's own retaliatory tariffs raise prices for its own consumers and create domestic deadweight loss.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Optimal Tariff for a Large Country vs. a Small Open Economy
questions.prompt_template: In the optional advanced analysis of a large importing country, the optimal ad valorem tariff rate is tau* = 1 / epsilon_s*, where epsilon_s* is the foreign export supply elasticity. Why does this formula imply tau* = 0 for a small open economy, and why is even a large country's optimal tariff risky in practice?

hints.text: Think about what foreign export supply elasticity epsilon_s* approaches when a small country faces a fixed world price P_w.
Also consider what the optimal tariff formula assumes about foreign trading partners' policy response.

options_template.text: For a small country, epsilon_s* approaches 0 (so tau* = 0); for a large country, tariffs cannot change the world price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity-Limit Reversal): As epsilon_s* approaches 0, 1 / epsilon_s* approaches infinity, not zero; a small country faces perfectly elastic foreign supply (epsilon_s* -> infinity).

options_template.text: For a small country, foreign export supply is perfectly elastic (epsilon_s* -> infinity), so tau* = 0 and no terms-of-trade gain is possible; for a large country, the formula assumes foreign partners do not retaliate with counter-tariffs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A small price-taking country faces epsilon_s* -> infinity, making any tariff strictly welfare-reducing (tau* = 0). A large country can gain terms-of-trade (Delta P_w * M_t), but foreign retaliation typically leaves both nations worse off.

options_template.text: For a small country, deadweight loss is zero; for a large country, terms-of-trade gains always exceed deadweight loss even after foreign retaliation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Retaliation-Proof Myth): A small country suffers positive deadweight loss (B + D), and retaliatory trade wars typically erase a large country's terms-of-trade gain.

options_template.text: For a small country, tau* = 1; for a large country, tau* = 0 because large countries never import goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Formula & Trade Reversal): Large economies import extensively, and tau* = 1 / epsilon_s* approaches 0 for a small price-taking country.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Trade Adjustment and Worker Support Policies
questions.title: Open Trade Paired with Targeted Worker Adjustment Assistance
questions.prompt_template: Suppose opening to free trade lowers apparel prices for millions of households while displacing workers at several domestic textile mills. Which policy package best preserves the net social surplus gains from trade while addressing concentrated worker hardship?

hints.text: Distinguish between *whether* to help displaced workers and *how* to help them at lowest social cost.
Compare permanent border tariffs against keeping trade open while funding targeted worker retraining and relocation assistance.

options_template.text: Impose prohibitive tariffs on imported apparel so that no domestic textile worker ever needs to change jobs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Autarky-Preservation Cost): Prohibitive tariffs destroy the entire free-trade net social surplus triangle and permanently tax millions of households.

options_template.text: Keep borders open to capture the net social surplus gains from lower prices, and use targeted domestic policies such as worker retraining and relocation assistance to support displaced workers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Keeping trade open preserves the larger social pie (Delta TS > 0), while targeted retraining and adjustment programs directly aid displaced workers without distorting consumer prices or incurring permanent tariff deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Replace tariffs with import quotas whose licenses are given to foreign apparel exporters.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Foreign-Rent Transfer Error): Giving quota licenses to foreign exporters worsens domestic welfare loss from B + D to B + C + D without retraining workers.

options_template.text: Do nothing to support displaced workers because free trade eliminates all short-run adjustment costs automatically.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frictionless-Adjustment Myth): Chapter 14 explicitly recognizes sharp, concentrated short-run losses for displaced workers and distinguishes supporting workers from restricting trade.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Auctioning Import Licenses vs. Free Allocation to Domestic or Foreign Firms
questions.prompt_template: A government has already committed to enforcing a 10-ton import quota on steel (holding domestic price at $50 vs. P_w = $40, creating $100 in Area C quota rents). Compare the national welfare and fiscal outcomes of (1) auctioning the licenses competitively to domestic importers versus (2) giving the licenses away free to foreign exporters.

hints.text: Check who captures Area C ($100) under each allocation method.
Determine whether Area C stays inside the domestic economy or leaks abroad.

options_template.text: Both methods produce the exact same domestic net welfare loss ($50) and the exact same government revenue ($100).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Allocation-Irrelevance Fallacy): Giving licenses free to foreign exporters forfeits $100 in public revenue and leaks Area C abroad, tripling domestic net welfare loss from $50 to $150.

options_template.text: Auctioning the licenses captures Area C ($100) as domestic government revenue—matching a tariff's fiscal outcome and limiting domestic welfare loss to B + D ($50)—whereas giving licenses to foreign exporters transfers Area C abroad, widening domestic loss to B + C + D ($150).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Competitive license auctions convert quota rents into domestic treasury revenue just like a tariff, keeping domestic net welfare loss at B + D rather than B + C + D.

options_template.text: Giving licenses to foreign exporters lowers the domestic steel price back to $40, eliminating deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (License-Price Error): Regardless of who holds the 10-ton quota licenses, the 10-ton physical cap holds the domestic price at $50.

options_template.text: Auctioning the licenses doubles deadweight loss to $100 because domestic importers pass the auction fee on top of $50.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Pass-Through Error): The domestic market-clearing price for a 10-ton quota is fixed at $50 by domestic supply and demand; competitive bidders bid up to the $10 per-ton rent ($50 - $40) without raising the $50 market price.
